Native keeps the original realm names. Realm Identity combines the current sovereign rank with the realm's established name, using bellum_realm_names.xml for configured realms. Sovereign Title uses the current sovereign title's territorial name and rank. Cultural terminology applies to both Bellum modes. Temporary rebellion and feud names remain unchanged. Default: Sovereign Title.

Bellum Civile

Bellum Civile expands the politics of Calradia through court factions, feudal rights, family ambitions and negotiated warfare. Noble houses pursue their interests within the realm, remember how they have been treated and decide which causes deserve their support.{newline}{newline}At court, factions seek favorable laws and appointments. Beyond it, claims can become private feuds, and discontented houses can organize rebellions. Land has both an actual holder and a legal owner, allowing hereditary rights to survive conquest. Marriages and inheritances carry these rights between houses and can eventually unite or divide realms.{newline}{newline}The player takes part according to their position. A vassal can cultivate allies, lead a faction or pursue a title. A ruler appoints councillors, rewards service and manages the interests of the court. In foreign affairs, military success provides leverage for treaties involving land, wealth, prisoners and political concessions.{newline}{newline}Begin with {BC_CONCEPT_COURT_FACTIONS_AND_THE_CROWN_LINK}, {BC_CONCEPT_DE_JURE_RIGHTS_AND_DE_FACTO_CONTROL_LINK}, or {BC_CONCEPT_SUCCESSION_LAWS_AND_ELECTIVE_MANDATES_LINK}. Court Factions and the Crown

Court factions bring together noble houses with shared political interests. Each permanent realm has three: Nobility, Glory and Liberty. A house's circumstances, relationships and its leader's personality influence its affiliation.{newline}{newline}Nobility favors landed rights, legal claims, noble representation and dynastic ties. Glory seeks military achievement, successful campaigns and conquest. Liberty values trade, prosperity, peace and limits on royal power. Their members pursue these interests through policies, appointments and other court business.{newline}{newline}The ruling house is represented by the Crown. Each term, the ruler may spend influence to favor one faction or remain impartial. Favor aligns the ruler with that faction's applicable political objectives, including support for campaigns, treaty terms and claimed lands.{newline}{newline}The Factions tab shows each faction's leader, members, mood and current agenda. Players can choose their affiliation and, when offered leadership, direct the faction's business. Membership affects relations within the court, giving shared interests a personal as well as a political importance.{newline}{newline}{BC_CONCEPT_FACTION_MOOD_AND_POLITICAL_AGENDAS_LINK} explains how these interests become proposals. {BC_CONCEPT_REBEL_FACTIONS_AND_GRAND_COALITIONS_LINK} describes the movements that challenge royal authority by force.{newline}{newline}{BC_CONCEPT_BELLUM_CIVILE_LINK}
Faction Mood and Political Agendas

Faction mood measures how satisfied a court faction is with the government of the realm. Laws, landholding, prosperity, war and representation on the Privy Council shape its continuing outlook. Events such as appointments, concessions and broken promises bring more immediate approval or resentment.{newline}{newline}During each court term, a faction chooses an eligible agenda according to its interests, mood and opportunities. It may propose a policy, seek a council appointment or encourage a campaign or diplomatic agreement. A contented faction may sponsor an activity that benefits the realm; a disaffected one may organize obstruction or withhold cooperation.{newline}{newline}Political objectives give the realm a goal to pursue during the term. A faction seeking a campaign can encourage war support, while one seeking an alliance can lend its backing to the proposed agreement. Achieving the objective earns approval. Failure or neglect can deepen discontent, while changed circumstances may cancel an objective without blame.{newline}{newline}The faction's entry in the Factions tab displays its agenda and the reasons for its mood. These show both the immediate business before the court and the lasting conditions that the ruler may need to address.{newline}{newline}{BC_CONCEPT_BELLUM_CIVILE_LINK}
Leading a Court Faction

A faction leader directs the political efforts of its members. Leadership gives the player an opportunity to pursue shared interests while choosing which available cause deserves the faction's attention.{newline}{newline}At the opening of a term, the members present their preferred motion. The player may approve it, block it or spend influence to substitute another eligible proposal. The alternatives depend on the faction's mood and the opportunities available in the realm.{newline}{newline}Policy and council motions can grant a mandate to act. During its filing window, a policy mandate allows the leader to propose eligible business through the Policies menu, while a council mandate allows an appointment proceeding through the Privy Council. The resulting decision then follows the realm's normal deliberation and voting process.{newline}{newline}Members expect their leader to use the authority they have granted. Allowing an unused mandate to expire can damage relations with them. Pursuing the promised motion gives the faction its hearing, even when other houses ultimately oppose the result.{newline}{newline}Player rulers exercise their own authority through the dedicated kingdom menus and Crown Actions. Those actions remain available under their ordinary costs and requirements throughout the term.{newline}{newline}{BC_CONCEPT_BELLUM_CIVILE_LINK}
The Privy Council

The Privy Council gives nobles responsibility for the realm's military, diplomatic, administrative and clandestine affairs. Its offices provide their holders with influence and a salary, while their performance affects confidence in the Crown.{newline}{newline}The Marshal directs military affairs, the Chancellor attends to diplomacy and the court, the Seneschal oversees administration and feudal revenues, and the Spymaster conducts intrigue and counters hostile schemes. Larger realms can sustain additional advisory offices. Council seats are held by nobles serving the ruler.{newline}{newline}Competence measures the skills relevant to an office. Assignments direct the councillor's work toward particular duties, with their benefits and drawbacks explained on the office card. Appointment candidates also display their competence, helping the player weigh ability alongside political support.{newline}{newline}Controversy records failures associated with an office, while support reflects the councillor's standing among the court. A councillor can therefore be skilled yet politically isolated, or well connected despite a poor record. Dismissal and replacement affect both personal relations and faction approval. A new holder begins with the office's controversy cleared.{newline}{newline}NPC rulers relieve captured councillors and arrange eligible replacements. Player rulers decide how to handle their own captive officers. Open the Privy Council in the Factions tab to inspect offices, assignments and appointment proceedings.{newline}{newline}{BC_CONCEPT_BELLUM_CIVILE_LINK}
Laws and Political Deliberation

Laws shape the balance of power within a realm. They can strengthen the ruler, protect noble privileges or favor the prosperity of towns and villages. Houses judge proposed changes according to their interests and their confidence in the Crown.{newline}{newline}Court factions support, oppose or remain neutral toward individual policies. Their mood also affects their willingness to support centralizing measures: a pleased faction is more willing to entrust authority to the ruler. In the Policies menu, blue marks policies supported by the player's faction, red marks opposition and an unhighlighted card indicates neutrality.{newline}{newline}Important decisions in the player's realm allow a period of deliberation. During policy, fief, expulsion and council proceedings, the player can speak with clan leaders about their intended votes. Lords explain their reasons, and eligible persuasion or bribery can redirect their support.{newline}{newline}Where a decision permits it, the ruler may override opposition at an influence and relationship cost. The outcome can also affect relations between houses that supported or opposed one another.{newline}{newline}The Policies menu includes separate groups of succession laws, each with one active selection. {BC_CONCEPT_SUCCESSION_LAWS_AND_ELECTIVE_MANDATES_LINK} explains how these govern inheritance, elections and the duration of a ruler's mandate.{newline}{newline}{BC_CONCEPT_BELLUM_CIVILE_LINK}
Rebellious Intent

Rebellious Intent measures a house's willingness to challenge the ruler. It grows from grievances and ambitions, shaped by the clan leader's personality and the political circumstances of the realm.{newline}{newline}Poor relations with the sovereign, an unhappy court faction, failures of government, disputed rights and an unsatisfactory share of land can all encourage opposition. A ruler who keeps extensive estates while other houses remain underlanded may provoke particular resentment. Family ties, loyalty and a favorable position in the realm can instead encourage patience.{newline}{newline}As intent rises, a house becomes more inclined to organize or join a rebel movement. Its chosen cause gives that discontent a direction: independence, abdication or the installation of a claimant. The movement then gathers supporters and assesses its strength before issuing an ultimatum. A contested succession may offer an earlier opportunity to act.{newline}{newline}The reasons shown for rebellious intent help identify what matters to the house in question. Grants, reconciliation, effective government and political concessions can address those pressures. Faction mood influences the wider climate at court, while each house retains its own reasons for loyalty or rebellion.{newline}{newline}{BC_CONCEPT_BELLUM_CIVILE_LINK}
Rebel Factions and Grand Coalitions

Rebel factions organize houses around a demand they are prepared to enforce against the Crown. Independence movements seek to leave the realm. Abdication movements seek the removal of its ruler. Install Ruler factions support a claimant with a valid basis for taking the throne.{newline}{newline}Before war, a movement recruits supporters and prepares its challenge. When its leaders judge their position strong enough, they may issue an ultimatum. Refusal can turn the dispute into a civil war whose outcome determines the fate of that demand.{newline}{newline}A deeply unhappy court faction may also seek a grand coalition to remove the sovereign. Other court factions can join when their own hostility is sufficient, bringing several political interests behind the same challenge. These coalitions pursue abdication, with succession handled according to the resulting political settlement.{newline}{newline}Players can support the Crown or an eligible rebel cause. Their personal obligations matter: following a rebellious liege can place them against the sovereign, while remaining loyal to the Crown may offend that liege.{newline}{newline}{BC_CONCEPT_POLITICAL_POWER_AND_CALLS_TO_ARMS_LINK} explains how movements draw military support. {BC_CONCEPT_CIVIL_WAR_SETTLEMENTS_AND_TRIBUNALS_LINK} describes the consequences of victory and defeat.{newline}{newline}{BC_CONCEPT_BELLUM_CIVILE_LINK}
Political Power and Calls to Arms

A house draws power from its soldiers, influence and political connections. Vassals, marriage allies and close friends can bring additional strength to its cause, allowing a dispute between a few nobles to divide a realm.{newline}{newline}The balance-of-power display combines a house's own military strength and influence with projected support from eligible allies. The tooltip separates these contributions. A house connected through several ties is counted once, and its expected support reflects its circumstances and existing commitments.{newline}{newline}When an internal conflict begins, eligible title-vassals, same-realm marriage allies and close friends receive calls to arms. They weigh their obligations, relationships, personality, the cause and the apparent strength of each side. Court affiliation can influence that decision, while the summons itself arises from those personal or feudal ties.{newline}{newline}Players receive their side choices directly. A player leading a cause also receives reports of allies accepting or refusing the call. Refusing an immediate liege can damage relations even when the player remains loyal to the Crown.{newline}{newline}These responses turn projected support into actual participation. Mercenary houses serving the Crown are excluded from private-feud summons because their military service belongs to their employer.{newline}{newline}{BC_CONCEPT_BELLUM_CIVILE_LINK}
Claim Feuds and Private Wars

A claim feud is a dispute between noble houses over a title. The claimant presses their rights, gathers supporters and increases pressure on the holder. As the dispute develops, the ruler may be asked to settle it.{newline}{newline}While the feud remains political, the Crown can judge between the parties, abstain or suppress the issue. A house that rejects the outcome may resort to arms, creating a private war within the realm.{newline}{newline}The disputed holding becomes the war's objective. Battles, occupation and captivity contribute War Score, while uninterrupted control of the objective builds additional leverage over time. Victory or concession settles the conflict according to its demands. White peace leaves the dispute unresolved and returns the participating houses to the parent realm.{newline}{newline}The player can initiate eligible claim feuds through the Factions tab. A player who joined as a supporter can use Leave before or during the fighting. Wartime withdrawal returns their house and possessions to the realm and creates an Oathbreaker grievance among their former allies.{newline}{newline}A foreign attack can prompt the Crown to enforce peace upon eligible private feuds, bringing the houses back together for the realm's defense. Player rulers select this action through Crown Actions, subject to its influence cost and requirements.{newline}{newline}{BC_CONCEPT_BELLUM_CIVILE_LINK}
Civil-War Settlements and Tribunals

An internal war ends by resolving its political demand or abandoning the struggle. Victory may secure independence, remove a sovereign, install a claimant or settle a private feud. Concession accepts the opposing side's outcome, while white peace leaves the dispute unresolved and reunites the realm.{newline}{newline}War Score provides military leverage, and exhaustion influences the willingness to continue. Civil wars and private feuds use these measures to reach their own settlements. An open rebellion against the Crown must follow those conflict rules; royal peace enforcement applies to eligible private feuds.{newline}{newline}After a victory that permits judgment, the ruler may hold a tribunal over defeated houses. Pardon offers reconciliation. Confiscation takes land and leaves a lasting grievance. Eligible landless houses may be exiled, and execution brings consequences among the condemned noble's relatives and associates.{newline}{newline}The tribunal belongs to the authority established by the settlement. An abdication war must first determine the new ruler. Successful independence establishes a separate realm and leaves the former sovereign outside the new ruler's jurisdiction.{newline}{newline}The settlement closes the war, while its rewards and punishments become part of the houses' political memory. A merciful victory can restore cooperation; severe reprisals may leave a future generation with reasons to seek revenge.{newline}{newline}{BC_CONCEPT_BELLUM_CIVILE_LINK}
De Jure Rights and De Facto Control

De facto control means actual possession of a title. De jure ownership means the recognized legal right to it. Bellum Civile records both, allowing a conqueror to hold land while another house retains its hereditary rights.{newline}{newline}The de facto holder exercises present authority and draws their displayed rank from their highest controlled title. De jure ownership supports legal inheritance and the established hierarchy of the land. A house holding both enjoys full ownership.{newline}{newline}For example, capturing a castle gives the conqueror possession while its legal title may remain with the former owner. A later royal award gives the recipient control, but the rights conveyed depend on what the grantor actually owns. The former legal house can therefore remain part of the dispute after the military campaign has ended.{newline}{newline}The Hierarchy displays separate de facto and de jure trees. In title listings, "de facto only" identifies possession without legal ownership, while "de jure only" identifies legal ownership without possession.{newline}{newline}{BC_CONCEPT_CLAIMS_AND_CLAIM_FABRICATION_LINK}, inheritance, lawful transfers and {BC_CONCEPT_DE_JURE_DRIFT_LINK} provide ways for rights and control to change. Consult both trees when deciding which title to pursue and whose interests the action will affect.{newline}{newline}{BC_CONCEPT_BELLUM_CIVILE_LINK}
The Feudal Hierarchy and Service

The feudal hierarchy organizes land and authority through baronies, counties, duchies, kingdoms and empires. Baronies correspond to towns and castles. Higher titles group territory and place lesser title holders beneath superior lords.{newline}{newline}A duke may therefore possess a few personal estates while other houses hold the counties and baronies under the duchy. Personal wealth comes from the lands and rights the house controls; political strength also depends on the obligations and support of its vassals.{newline}{newline}Feudal service directs revenues through the hierarchy and helps determine military authority. With restricted feudal army calls enabled, ordinary nobles summon forces according to their position and rights. The sovereign and the Marshal have broader authority to assemble the realm's host.{newline}{newline}The de jure tree shows the lawful arrangement of titles, while the de facto tree shows current authority. Conquest, inheritance and reorganization can produce differences between them, affecting who receives service and which houses consider their rights infringed.{newline}{newline}These ties matter during internal conflict as well. Direct title-vassals can be summoned by their liege, and refusing that obligation may damage relations. The Hierarchy helps the player understand both the resources attached to a title and the political relationships that come with it.{newline}{newline}{BC_CONCEPT_BELLUM_CIVILE_LINK}
Claims and Claim Fabrication

A claim gives a house a recognized argument for acquiring a title. Claims can arise through marriage, inheritance, dispossession or fabrication, and their strength affects contests over land and rank.{newline}{newline}Strong claims represent more substantial rights than weak claims. They may descend to the next generation as weak claims, while weak claims expire with their carrier. Marriage can bring claims to the spouse's parental-house titles into the receiving house, making family connections valuable to future ambitions.{newline}{newline}Fabrication offers a way to establish a weak claim by preparing a legal case and forged documents. It costs gold, influence and time. Checks take place as precedents are gathered, charters prepared and final documents completed. Each uses the same risk formula, based on current skills and council conditions.{newline}{newline}An early failure creates a private setback. The player can fund the repair, repeat the affected work at the cost of time, or abandon the attempt. Repeating that stage avoids rerolling its failed check. Failure at the final checkpoint exposes the forgery and brings a scandal; success grants the claim.{newline}{newline}The Hierarchy shows claims and fabrication progress. Its Renounce action lets the player surrender an eligible claim to a title they do not currently control, removing the associated claimant grievance where that claim caused it.{newline}{newline}{BC_CONCEPT_BELLUM_CIVILE_LINK}
Usurpation, Revocation and Title Grants

Usurpation allows a claimant with sufficient control to assume a title. It ordinarily requires a valid claim, the necessary resources and control of more than half the relevant subordinate territory. The title's surviving hierarchy determines which holdings count toward that requirement.{newline}{newline}Revocation allows an immediate superior to demand an eligible subordinate title. The revoker needs the appropriate de facto authority, a claim and the required influence. A holder who refuses can defend their position through a private war.{newline}{newline}Grants transfer eligible possessions or titles to another house. A higher-title grant can give the recipient authority over existing vassals, while those vassals retain their own holdings. A suitable baronial grant to a companion can establish a new noble house with land and obligations of its own.{newline}{newline}Each transfer conveys rights according to the grantor's legal position. A grant of full ownership can settle both possession and title; an award of occupied land can leave another house's de jure rights intact. Fiefs temporarily held by the Crown for distribution remain subject to their existing legal history.{newline}{newline}Select a title in the Hierarchy to inspect its available actions. Their tooltips explain the costs, authority and control needed for the particular case. {BC_CONCEPT_CLAIM_FEUDS_AND_PRIVATE_WARS_LINK} describes what can follow when a demand is resisted.{newline}{newline}{BC_CONCEPT_BELLUM_CIVILE_LINK}
Creating and Reorganizing Titles

Creating a title brings existing territory under a new legal authority. A lord can ordinarily form an upper title from at least two contiguous child titles of the same rank, provided the necessary ownership, authority and resources are available.{newline}{newline}The player selects eligible territory through the Hierarchy and can name the new title before confirming it. When the selected children already belong to another de jure parent, the actor generally needs both legal ownership and actual control to detach them. Reorganization must also preserve the rights of independent vassals and a coherent hierarchy for the existing Crown.{newline}{newline}Other houses' claims can survive as a political concern even when they do not block the change. Overriding those interests creates resentment for disregarding ancestral claims. An active feud over an affected title prevents its dissolution or rearrangement while the dispute is being pursued.{newline}{newline}Dissolving an eligible upper title leaves its subordinate titles in existence and places them in the appropriate hierarchy. Surviving titles keep their relevant legal history; a newly created upper title begins its own.{newline}{newline}The structure also shapes inheritance. Creating coequal sovereign titles can make later separation possible when eligible heirs receive them. A higher legal title binding those Crowns can instead preserve their place within one realm.{newline}{newline}{BC_CONCEPT_BELLUM_CIVILE_LINK}
De Jure Drift

De jure drift gradually incorporates eligible titles into the legal hierarchy of the realm that controls them. It represents the acceptance of boundaries established by long possession, turning a lasting political arrangement into recognized law.{newline}{newline}Progress depends on the title's ownership and hierarchy conditions. The receiving title must be suitable and higher in rank: a county can become part of a duchy, while one kingdom cannot drift beneath another kingdom of equal rank. The Hierarchy tooltip shows progress and explains unmet conditions.{newline}{newline}Each title keeps its own clock. If a barony has already progressed for several years when its county becomes eligible, both continue on their respective schedules. Temporary separation during a civil war or private feud preserves progress tied to the permanent realm.{newline}{newline}Lawful reorganization also preserves the relevant history of surviving titles. A barony can retain its progress after being placed under a new county. A newly created upper title, however, begins its own history rather than taking over the elapsed time of a dissolved predecessor.{newline}{newline}Drift takes many years, with its duration set through the mod options. During that time, the de facto and de jure trees continue to show the difference between present control and established legal boundaries.{newline}{newline}{BC_CONCEPT_BELLUM_CIVILE_LINK}
Succession Laws and Elective Mandates

Succession laws determine who inherits authority when a ruler dies or leaves office. Hereditary realms follow a lawful personal line; elective realms choose among eligible candidates within their political community.{newline}{newline}Hereditary laws can favor the eldest descendant, the youngest, senior members of the dynasty or other eligible kin. Gender laws determine whether men and women are equally eligible, preferred in order or excluded. Personal rights can remain with an heir who has married into a foreign house.{newline}{newline}In elective realms, houses weigh the qualities favored by the electoral law alongside relationships and political interests. Standing nominations and support reveal the developing contest. The succession panel shows the candidates or hereditary line applicable to the realm.{newline}{newline}Elective mandates last for a fixed term or for life. A change between fixed durations retains the mandate's original start. Changing a lifetime mandate to a fixed term starts its clock when the reform is adopted; changing to lifetime removes its expiry. If the revised term has already elapsed, an election follows after notice.{newline}{newline}House inheritance follows the laws of its realm, while independent houses use cultural defaults. The Clan encyclopedia identifies the legal heirs. The option governing the player's playable-heir selection can allow a freer personal choice while the world continues to follow its legal succession rules.{newline}{newline}{BC_CONCEPT_BELLUM_CIVILE_LINK}
Regencies and Underage Heirs

A regency allows a noble house to pass to an underage heir while an adult governs on their behalf. The child is the lawful heir, and the regent serves as the acting leader until the ward reaches adulthood.{newline}{newline}A suitable adult relative can take the position. Where the house lacks an eligible adult, Bellum Civile provides a noble of the appropriate culture to maintain its administration. If the regent becomes unable to serve, another can take over the duty while the ward retains their succession rights.{newline}{newline}The regent's title identifies whom they serve. Entry into regency, changes of regent and the eventual handover are announced. At adulthood, the ward assumes leadership. A generated regent remains an ordinary member of the house afterward.{newline}{newline}With legal-heir enforcement enabled, the player can also experience a regency. An underage succession prompts the choice of an eligible regent to play, followed by a handover to the ward when they come of age. The timing follows the campaign's configured adulthood rules.{newline}{newline}The {BC_CONCEPT_SUCCESSION_LAWS_AND_ELECTIVE_MANDATES_LINK} article explains the laws that identify the heir before a regency becomes necessary.{newline}{newline}{BC_CONCEPT_BELLUM_CIVILE_LINK}
Dynastic Marriage

Dynastic marriages help houses secure heirs, build alliances, gain prestige and acquire claims. A promising match can strengthen a family's future even when its immediate benefit is a connection rather than land.{newline}{newline}When strategic marriage is enabled, both houses consider the proposed household arrangement. Healthy families can pursue status and useful political ties, while houses facing extinction place greater value on continuity and lower their expectations of prestige. Sending a relative to another house is weighed against what the connection offers in return.{newline}{newline}One spouse generally joins the other's house. Royal circumstances and particular arrangements can change that destination, and a spouse may retain personal rights to a Crown after moving. Marriage can also bring claims to parental-house titles into the receiving family.{newline}{newline}These ties encourage cooperation between houses and can improve the prospects of a formal alliance between realms. The diplomatic agreement is decided separately, giving rulers and their courts a further opportunity to support or oppose it.{newline}{newline}The player can discuss specific candidates through marriage dialogue and decides whether to accept proposals involving their own house. A suitable NPC match can be pursued again after a temporary obstacle, such as military service, has passed. Family health, relations and strategic value continue to shape the proposal.{newline}{newline}{BC_CONCEPT_BELLUM_CIVILE_LINK}
Cadet Branches and Divided Inheritances

Cadet branches are new noble houses formed from an existing family. In a divided inheritance, secondary heirs can receive estates and titles of their own, establishing separate households while retaining their common ancestry.{newline}{newline}The inheritance follows title groups and associated lands, with possessions reserved for the principal heir and suitable shares assigned to other eligible heirs. Available land, lawful rights and the structure of the estate determine which branches can be established.{newline}{newline}Most branches remain within their parent realm. When an independent ruler's inheritance contains qualifying coequal sovereign titles, a secondary heir may instead become an independent ruler. A landed duchy can separate through ordinary estate division, while multiple Crowns follow their own allocation of titles and vassal domains. Higher-title ownership and the legal structure can keep the inheritance together.{newline}{newline}An heir living in another house can retain personal succession rights. A later accession may establish a separate ruling house where required, with household membership and inherited possessions settled through that succession.{newline}{newline}The Clan encyclopedia shows family connections and succession information, while the Hierarchy shows the titles each branch holds. Claims and shared ancestry can continue to bind the houses together, offering grounds for cooperation or future disputes over their common inheritance.{newline}{newline}{BC_CONCEPT_BELLUM_CIVILE_LINK}
Personal Unions and the Separation of Crowns

A personal union forms when an existing sovereign lawfully inherits another Crown of equal rank. One ruler then holds both titles, and the inherited realm joins the heir's existing kingdom.{newline}{newline}The existing kingdom retains its government, laws, policies and court. The inherited realm's noble houses join it peacefully, mercenary contracts end, and compatible diplomatic commitments transfer. The inherited Crown and its legal vassal tree remain distinct within the combined realm's hierarchy.{newline}{newline}For example, a Vlandian sovereign who inherits Sturgia can govern both through Vlandia while also holding the Sturgian Crown. The Sturgian title tree survives, preserving the legal organization of its lands and vassals.{newline}{newline}That structure matters at the next inheritance. Eligible heirs may receive separate coequal Crowns and establish independent realms again. A fully held higher legal title binding the Crowns, such as an empire, can keep them together.{newline}{newline}These unions arise when a ruler dies under hereditary succession. Both realms must be independent, with their ruling houses holding legal ownership and actual control of their Crowns. Integration can wait while incompatible wars, hostage arrangements or conflicting political commitments remain unresolved, preserving the lawful heir's place in the succession.{newline}{newline}{BC_CONCEPT_CADET_BRANCHES_AND_DIVIDED_INHERITANCES_LINK} explains how title estates can pass to different heirs.{newline}{newline}{BC_CONCEPT_BELLUM_CIVILE_LINK}
Noble Mercenary Companies

Mercenary service offers ambitious nobles a path to wealth and distinction beyond their family's estates. Eligible adults who are not due to inherit under the partition plan may join a suitable company or found one of their own.{newline}{newline}A new company takes its identity and soldiers from its cultural surroundings. Its leader establishes a military household whose fortunes depend on service, contracts and campaigning. Opportunities are considered periodically, subject to family circumstances and the configured limits on company formation.{newline}{newline}Relatives of the player can pursue this career as well. A family member traveling with the player may ask for support or announce their intentions. The player can fund the venture, give a blessing, attempt persuasion or forbid the departure. Those choices affect the relationship, and a forceful refusal can lead to resentment or defiance. Relatives who are away can send word by letter.{newline}{newline}The company's encyclopedia entry records its founding history where known, including the founder and their origins. Relations with the parent house can preserve gratitude for help or resentment over opposition. Once serving as mercenaries, the company's obligations to a Crown follow its contract.{newline}{newline}{BC_CONCEPT_BELLUM_CIVILE_LINK}
War Will and Strategic Ambition

War Will measures a house's enthusiasm for warfare. With the War and Peace Revamp enabled, it helps determine when a clan is ready to support a new campaign or begins pressing for settlement.{newline}{newline}Peace allows enthusiasm to recover. Campaigning, losses, captivity and the burden of several fronts can reduce it, while victories, defensive resolve and political interests influence the response. Houses within the same realm can therefore differ in how eagerly they support continued war.{newline}{newline}When a house is ready to fight, strategic considerations guide its choice of enemy. Claims, borders, cultural ties, rivalries, prosperity and military danger all matter. A vulnerable neighbor may offer an opportunity, while existing enemies can make another front too costly.{newline}{newline}Alliances, trade agreements, marriages and hostage pledges discourage aggression according to their political importance. Court objectives can encourage a particular campaign, lending support to a target that serves the faction's interests.{newline}{newline}The reasons accompanying a war proposal explain these ambitions. Later in the conflict, enthusiasm influences the desire for peace, while War Score and treaty terms determine the settlement a house considers worthwhile. {BC_CONCEPT_WAR_SCORE_AND_EXHAUSTION_LINK} explains how those pressures develop during a campaign.{newline}{newline}{BC_CONCEPT_BELLUM_CIVILE_LINK}
War Score and Exhaustion

War Score measures the military leverage gained during a conflict. Battles, occupation, successful raids and captured nobles contribute to the balance, showing which side has earned the stronger position for settlement.{newline}{newline}Some leverage lasts only while its source remains. Releasing or rescuing a prisoner removes the value of that captivity, and recovering occupied land changes the territorial balance. Each village can provide raid credit only once for a side during the conflict.{newline}{newline}In a private feud, holding the disputed objective earns additional score over time. Losing control clears that side's accumulated objective advantage, and the new controller begins building its own.{newline}{newline}Peace acceptance also reflects campaign length and enthusiasm. Early in a war, lords tend to resist settling before achieving a useful result. That reluctance diminishes with time and weakens as enthusiasm approaches exhaustion. A long campaign adds further pressure to end the struggle.{newline}{newline}White peace becomes possible when the score is close to even and both sides are deeply exhausted. A clearer military advantage supports concession or demands. Internal wars use these pressures to resolve their political causes; foreign wars turn them into bargaining power in the Peace Parley.{newline}{newline}War Score tooltips show the sources of leverage. Council assessments explain whether the proposed terms offer a settlement the participating houses will accept.{newline}{newline}{BC_CONCEPT_BELLUM_CIVILE_LINK}
Peace Parleys and Treaty Terms

The Peace Parley allows warring realms to turn military results into a negotiated agreement. With the War and Peace Revamp enabled, both councils assess the terms according to leverage, exhaustion and their political interests.{newline}{newline}Player rulers can edit demands and offerings involving fiefs, prisoners, wealth and political concessions. Player vassals support or oppose the agreement through their council position and influence commitment. Rulers then decide whether to accept their council's judgment or pay the applicable cost to override opposition.{newline}{newline}War Score supplies the demand budget. Offerings provide additional bargaining credit at a reduced value and within a cap, allowing one side to concede something useful in exchange for a stronger demand elsewhere. Excessive drafts show overwhelming opposition and must be brought within the available budget before they can be imposed.{newline}{newline}Victorious houses expect the treaty to make worthwhile use of their success. Territorial demands, reparations and tribute offer different ways to claim those gains, subject to what is available and affordable. Defeated houses weigh the burden of concessions against the prospects of continued resistance.{newline}{newline}Internal wars use a restricted parley focused on white peace or concession to the conflict's demand. Its result follows the rules of the rebellion or feud being settled.{newline}{newline}Open negotiations through the Diplomacy menu and inspect each council's assessment to understand which terms encourage agreement or provoke resistance.{newline}{newline}{BC_CONCEPT_BELLUM_CIVILE_LINK}
Hostages and Pledges of Peace

A hostage pledge secures peace by placing a blood relative of one ruler in the other realm's custody. The family member's safety gives the supplying house a powerful reason to preserve the agreement.{newline}{newline}Peace parleys can demand or offer an eligible relative for one hundred days by default. The mod configuration menu sets the duration of new pledges; existing agreements keep their promised term. Their position in the relevant succession determines the pledge's value, and children can serve as hostages. The captive remains in their own house while being held in an eligible stronghold of the receiving realm.{newline}{newline}Active treaty custody prevents ordinary ransom and escape. The encyclopedia and Clan menu identify the captive as a peace hostage, and ransom brokers explain the diplomatic reason for their detention.{newline}{newline}At expiry, the hostage is returned. Replacement of either recorded ruling house can also end the arrangement. War breaks the pledge and requires a decision about the captive: release, continued ordinary imprisonment or execution. NPC rulers choose according to personality and circumstances, while player captors receive a choice. Ordinary prisoners can again be ransomed, escape or be rescued.{newline}{newline}Dedicated dungeon dialogue lets a player captor honorably return a hostage early or order their execution, with consequences for relations and honor. If the other realm also holds a hostage, its ruler determines that person's fate in response.{newline}{newline}{BC_CONCEPT_BELLUM_CIVILE_LINK}
Client Kingdoms and Liberty Desire

A client kingdom keeps its ruler and identity while accepting a stronger realm's authority over foreign affairs. Its suzerain provides protection, and the client follows its lead in diplomacy and war.{newline}{newline}Clientage maintains an alliance and trade relationship between the realms. The client joins the suzerain's wars and peaces, with its independent diplomacy restricted by that obligation. A ruler may accept this position through a treaty or seek protection during a desperate defensive war. Accepting such an appeal includes joining the client's defense.{newline}{newline}The suzerain can strengthen the relationship by granting eligible personally held land. Peace terms can also recognize qualifying territory occupied by a client, allowing it to retain gains from a shared campaign.{newline}{newline}Liberty Desire measures the pressure for independence. Relative strength, relations, personality, burdens, claims and political conditions determine how tolerable the arrangement feels. Generous treatment and good relations can support loyalty alongside military dominance.{newline}{newline}A client seeking liberation must also judge its military prospects and readiness. Crown preparations can encourage that effort, while the eventual declaration follows the liberation requirements. If the suzerain collapses, its clients are released.{newline}{newline}The Diplomacy overview identifies client relationships and provides a Liberty Desire tooltip showing the pressures at work.{newline}{newline}{BC_CONCEPT_BELLUM_CIVILE_LINK}
Relations, Kinship and Political Memory

Relations combine personal affinities, current circumstances and memories of past dealings. These explain why friendship can endure hardship and why a political injury can remain important years after the event.{newline}{newline}Among nobles, personality and culture contribute an enduring foundation. Kinship supplies a family bond, using the strongest applicable relationship. Political conditions such as shared allegiance, court affiliation, contested titles and prisoner custody add motives that change as the situation changes.{newline}{newline}Event memories record assistance, betrayal, shared battles, political support and punishment. Ordinary temporary memories retain their effect for their duration, then expire. The length reflects the event's significance and the configured memory-duration setting.{newline}{newline}Personal memories concern particular characters. House memories belong to the families involved and survive changes of clan leader, allowing a successor to inherit gratitude or resentment from an earlier generation.{newline}{newline}Relatives within the same clan have individual relationships, and notables remember relevant dealings in their communities. Their opinions can therefore reflect both familiar ties and the player's actions.{newline}{newline}The encyclopedia relation tooltip lists the active motives and memories. It helps the player identify a temporary grievance, an ongoing political dispute or a lasting family bond, and decide which relationships can be improved by changing the circumstances.{newline}{newline}{BC_CONCEPT_BELLUM_CIVILE_LINK}
Intrigue and Proxy Warfare

Intrigue allows rulers to influence another realm through discreet intervention. Agents can undermine confidence at court, assist rebel movements or carry resources to those opposing a foreign Crown.{newline}{newline}Player rulers dispatch clan companions on time-limited clandestine missions. NPC rulers can undertake their own operations when the relevant setting is enabled. The available opportunity and the agent's ability to complete the mission shape its prospects.{newline}{newline}The Spymaster directs the realm's expertise in intrigue and resistance to hostile schemes. Competence and assignment affect offensive and defensive efforts; in the absence of a Spymaster, the ruler supplies the relevant direction.{newline}{newline}Successful assistance can strengthen an existing cause or deepen political discontent. The supported houses still make their decisions according to their own interests, giving sponsors a reason to understand the conflict before investing in it.{newline}{newline}Discovery can expose the ruler behind an operation and bring political consequences. Captivity or a change in the targeted conflict can also interrupt the mission. Intrigue is therefore an investment in influence over an uncertain situation, with its value depending on the divisions already present in the foreign realm.{newline}{newline}{BC_CONCEPT_BELLUM_CIVILE_LINK}
Bellum Civile Options

Bellum Civile's mod configuration menu controls optional systems and adjustable campaign rules. Its settings cover political timing, inheritance, marriage, relationship memories, warfare and interface elements.{newline}{newline}These articles describe the relevant systems when enabled. Action tooltips and the configuration menu show current requirements and costs, while configurable figures given in the guide describe their defaults.{newline}{newline}Some options affect presentation; others change how the campaign works. Disabling the War and Peace Revamp restores the ordinary war-and-peace path. Allowing free playable-heir selection changes the player's choice while other houses continue to follow legal succession. Settings that require a restart identify that requirement in their descriptions.{newline}{newline}When using other mods, follow Bellum's compatibility guidance for overlapping features. Diplomacy's non-aggression pacts and Bellum's hostage pledges, for example, are separate arrangements with their own rules. The compatibility warning identifies the settings recommended for using the mods together.{newline}{newline}{BC_CONCEPT_BELLUM_CIVILE_LINK}
